note: The known answer. Written by hand from the fixtures, not recorded from a
run: an expectation copied out of the instrument it is meant to check
would agree with the instrument no matter what the instrument did.
Counts above one are deliberate and are explained in 'why'.
ruff is a second instrument over the same trees. The clean tree must be
empty for the whole selection the ladder ever asks for; the dirty tree
must produce at least these codes, so that a ruff invocation that
silently does nothing -- wrong flags, wrong target version, a cache hit
-- cannot be mistaken for a clean tree.
Four hand-computed points on the scoring contract, checked against a
synthetic observation bundle rather than a real one.

why.collections-abc-alias: 2 = the `from collections import Iterable` statement + the `collections.Sized` attribute; the rule has an import arm and an attribute arm
why.dynamic-legacy-access: 5 = one per arm of the rule that the fixture spells: importlib.import_module('numpy.random'), getattr(random, 'shuffle'), sys.modules['numpy.random'], np.random.__dict__['rand'] and operator.attrgetter('seed')(np.random). The rule counts the fetch, not the call, because a fetched function can be stored and called anywhere; the eval/exec arm is rehearsed in check_exec_and_dynamic rather than here, because a string of source in this fixture would also be scanned as source and the two counts would be hard to read apart.
why.dynamic-retired-name: 5 = one per arm, over the names step 2 retires rather than step 1's: getattr(np, 'flo' + 'at'), np.__dict__['int'], vars(np)['object'], sys.modules['sklearn.externals'] and importlib.import_module('sklearn.grid_search'). The getattr site assembles the attribute from two literals, so the rule reads it as numpy.* and charges for the module it reaches into rather than the name it takes -- which is the whole point, since the name is not there to read. The two module-fetch arms are narrower than the others: they fire only for a module that is gone, so sys.modules['numpy'] in the clean tree is not a finding.
why.global-rng-seed: 2 = skutil/rng.py + the code cell of doc/examples/demo.ipynb, which proves notebooks are scanned and that %magics do not stop the parse
why.hot-path-row-iteration: 2 = a nested pair of `for ... in range(...)` inside filter_collinearity; each iteration expression counts once
why.invalid-string-escape: 2 = skutil/patterns.py + skutil/_speedups.pyx, the second of which would stop `ast` dead and so proves the tokenizer path ran
why.matplotlib-ambient-rcparams: 2 = the `rcParams[...] = ...` assignment arm + the `sns.set_style(...)` call arm
why.numpy-removed-alias: 3 = the `from numpy import float as npfloat` import arm + the `np.float` attribute arm + the `npfloat` Name arm
why.pandas-inplace-kwarg: 2 = inplace=True and inplace=False; step 6 gates the keyword whatever its value, step 2 gates only the True
why.pandas-object-dtype-blind: 2 = the bare `df.dtypes == 'object'` compare arm + the `select_dtypes(include=['object'])` call arm; the near_misses that pair each with a 'str' test (in frames.py and clean/modern.py) must not fire
why.py2-builtin: 2 = the `long` Name arm + the `.iteritems()` attribute arm
why.sklearn-load-boston: 2 = the import arm + the call arm
why.stdlib-global-rng: 2 = the random.shuffle(...) call + the getattr(random, 'shuffle') fetch, which names the same function and so is the same violation
